\section[An explicit quartic definition]{An explicit quartic definition of the integers}
\label{sec:quartics}

We now give the second final polynomial of this manuscript. Its arithmetic
source uses the base residual compiler of Section~\ref{sec:degree8-original},
with the reciprocal logarithms and mixed precisions proved below. A fresh
quadratic lift and explicit rational solution maps then give the following
fully expanded sum of squares.

\begin{theorem}[An explicit quartic definition]\label{thm:quartic}
With the arithmetic inputs of Section~\ref{sec:degree8-original}, the
coefficient file specified below defines an integer polynomial $\Phi$ of
total degree $4$, with $135\,721$ nonzero monomials in $12\,504$ variables.
For every $q\in\Q$,
\[
 q\in\Z\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \exists(w_1,\ldots,w_{12503})\in\Q^{12503},\qquad
 \Phi(q,w_1,\ldots,w_{12503})=0.
\]
Thus there are $12\,503$ existential witnesses in addition to the input.
Every listed variable occurs in the expanded polynomial, and
\[
 \|\Phi\|_\infty=685783949153203534233601<2^{80}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\subsection{Literal specification and coefficient file}

The companion repository directory \nolinkurl{quartics/quartic-12504/}
contains the complete coefficient table \nolinkurl{polynomial.expanded.txt}.
Its gzip copy has identical uncompressed bytes. After one comment line,
each line contains a nonzero signed integer coefficient followed by a
nondecreasing list of variable indices. An index repeated $e$ times denotes
exponent $e$; a coefficient with no indices is the constant term. Thus
\texttt{-6 0 2 2} denotes $-6X_0X_2^2$. The input is always $X_0$.
Like terms are collected and the lines are ordered lexicographically by
their index lists. The witness indices are assigned by occurrence frequency;
the file \nolinkurl{variable-map.json} records the exact relabeling.

The uncompressed coefficient file has $3\,239\,486$ bytes, including its
comment and line endings. Its SHA-256 digest is
\begin{center}\footnotesize\ttfamily
7f5aa3117af82a0b323f0a4e74a18599204f5540408106d3ce99612b5ed830ca.
\end{center}
This is a literal finite specification of every coefficient. No unspecified
auxiliary constant or choice of witnesses enters the coefficient table.

\subsection{The reciprocal comparison source}
\label{subsec:quartic-source}

We retain the arithmetic inputs, curve, generator, forty-one contacts,
scalar height batch, and twenty-four-squaring anchor of
Section~\ref{sec:degree8-original}. In particular, throughout this section
\[
 K=\Q(\sqrt2),\qquad d=3-\sqrt2,\qquad D=d^2=11-6\sqrt2,
 \qquad E:y^2=x^3-Dx,
\]
and $H=H_*$ is exactly the constant of Theorem~\ref{hyp:o8-height};
the height exponent remains $24$. Each element of $K$ is represented by
its two rational coefficients. Field multiplication and inversion mean
\[
 (a_0,a_1)(b_0,b_1)=(a_0b_0+2a_1b_1,a_0b_1+a_1b_0),\qquad
 a^{-1}=\frac{(a_0,-a_1)}{a_0^2-2a_1^2}\quad(a\ne0).
\]
The denominator is nonzero by the irrationality of $\sqrt2$.

There are two arithmetic changes to the base compiler. We use a different
finite approximation to the same formal logarithm, and impose precision
$16$ on the beta numerator and its alternate comparison. The common
denominator and the three Lucas numerators retain precision $64$.
The old and new finite approximations are not identical polynomials.
Their arithmetic interpretations must therefore be proved separately;
changing the source digest would not prove this revision.

\begin{lemma}[Reciprocal logarithm and its error]
\label{lem:quartic-reciprocal-log}
Put $f=1/x$, $z=-x/y$, and define
\[
 a_0=1,\qquad a_1=-\frac25,\qquad
 a_j=\frac{4j-5}{4j+1}a_{j-1}\quad(j\ge2),\qquad
 G(w)=\sum_{j\ge0}a_jw^j.
\]
On the formal branch at the identity,
\[
 \log_E(z)=zG(Df^2).
\]
For every $J\ge0$ put $G_J(w)=\sum_{j=0}^{J}a_jw^j$.
For $e\in\{16,64\}$, set $m=e/4$ and
\[
 G_{m-1}(w)=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}a_jw^j,\qquad
 L_e(z,f)=zG_{m-1}(Df^2).
\]
Let $p>76176$ be split and choose either place above it. If the point is
nonidentity and lies in the formal group at that place, so
$r=v_p(z)\ge1$ and $v_p(f)>0$, then
\[
 v_p\bigl(\log_E(z)-L_e(z,f)\bigr)\ge(4m+1)r,
 \qquad \frac{L_e(z,f)}{\log_E(z)}\in1+p^e\Z_p.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
The curve equation gives
\[
 f=z^2(1-Df^2),\qquad w=Df^2,\qquad Dz^4=\frac{w}{(1-w)^2}.
\]
Coefficient comparison in the defining recurrence gives
\[
 4w(1-w)G'(w)+(1+w)G(w)=1-w.
\]
Indeed the coefficient of $w$ is $5a_1+a_0=-1$, and each later
coefficient gives $(4j+1)a_j=(4j-5)a_{j-1}$. Differentiating the
curve identity yields $z\,dw/dz=4w(1-w)/(1+w)$. Consequently
\[
 \frac{d}{dz}\{zG(w)\}=\frac{1-w}{1+w}
                   =(1+4Dz^4)^{-1/2}.
\]
The square root has constant term one. This is the normalized invariant
differential for $z$, and $zG(w)$ has zero constant term, which proves
the formal identity.

At the stated place, $D$ is a unit and the formal branch gives
$v_p(f)=2r$, hence $v_p(w)=4r$. The denominator of $a_j$, for $j\ge1$,
divides $5\prod_{k=2}^j(4k+1)$ and therefore divides $(4j+1)!$.
Thus
\[
 v_p(a_j)\ge-v_p((4j+1)!)\ge-\frac{4j+1}{p-1}.
\]
For $j\ge m$ with $4j+1<p$, the coefficient is $p$-integral and
$v_p(a_jw^j)\ge4mr$. Otherwise $j\ge19044$, so $3j\ge4m$ and
$(4j+1)/(p-1)\le j$. Therefore
\[
 v_p(a_jw^j)\ge4jr-j\ge4mr.
\]
These lower bounds tend to infinity. They control the entire infinite
tail, including terms whose denominators are divisible by $p$.
Multiplication by $z$ proves the first estimate. Formal logarithm isometry
gives $v_p(\log_E(z))=r$, and proves the relative estimate.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Global nonvanishing]
\label{lem:quartic-reciprocal-nonzero}
For every $f\in K$ and every $J\ge2$,
\[
                 G_J(Df^2)\ne0.
\]
In particular $L_e(z,f)\ne0$ whenever $z\ne0$ and $e\in\{16,64\}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $\nu_2$ be the rational exponent-of-two valuation and put
\[
 v(a+b\sqrt2)=\tfrac12\nu_2(a^2-2b^2)
             =\min\{\nu_2(a),\nu_2(b)+\tfrac12\}.
\]
The two terms in the norm have valuations of opposite parity when finite.
Norm multiplicativity and the displayed minimum prove the valuation
identities. Its finite values lie in $\tfrac12\Z$, and $v(D)=0$.
Every $a_j$ with $j\ge1$ has valuation one, because $a_1=-2/5$ and
all subsequent recurrence factors have odd numerator and denominator.
If $f=0$, the assertion is immediate. If $t=v(f)\ge0$, the constant
term of $G_J(Df^2)$ is uniquely least in valuation. If $t<0$, then
$t\le-1/2$ and the nonconstant valuations $1+2jt$ strictly decrease;
the last is at most $1-J<0$, below the constant term as well. In either
case a uniquely least term proves nonvanishing. No good-reduction
assumption at two is used.
\end{proof}

For the moment use the full point charts of the base compiler. At each
contact let $Q_0$ be the common private primary point and let $Q_1,Q_2,Q_3,Q_4$
be the points for $\beta,\xi,\tau,\zeta$. Replace their logarithms by
$L_{64}$ at $Q_0,Q_2,Q_3,Q_4$ and by $L_{16}$ at $Q_1$.
The primary ratios are $C_i=L_{e_i}(Q_i)/L_{64}(Q_0)$.
Keep every subtraction chart, its nonzero-abscissa guard, the common
auxiliary point, and all eleven order-one field tests. In the original
field-test order, use
\[
 (\underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{11},16,64,64,64,64,16,64,64,64).
\]
The first four later entries test $C_i$ against the proxies; the last
five are the alternate comparisons, beginning with the common denominator
point. Each field expression $A+B\sqrt2$ gives the same two rational tests
$\varepsilon B,A+B\theta$, after the initial root-error test. Their orders are
\[
 (\underbrace{1,\ldots,1}_{23},16,16,
   \underbrace{64,\ldots,64}_{8},16,16,
   \underbrace{64,\ldots,64}_{6}).
\]
The scalar batch still has orders $(1,1,1,1,48,48)$.

\begin{theorem}[Arithmetic interpretation of the revised source]
\label{thm:quartic-source-arithmetic}
With the arithmetic inputs and conventions of
Section~\ref{sec:degree8-original}, the reciprocal comparison system just
specified has rational witnesses at input $X\in\Q$ exactly when $X\in\Z$.
The same assertion holds for its compressed primary-chart presentation
in Lemma~\ref{lem:quartic-compressed-primary}.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Begin with an arbitrary rational solution and any $p>76176$ at which
a raw contact has odd valuation. No ordinary-prime condition is assumed
in this direction. Put $R=v_p(r)$ for that raw contact. The constant-left
norm and pole argument of the base compiler first excludes $R<0$ and then
gives $v_p(X)> (e-1)R\ge e-1$ for each rational test $X$ of assigned
order $e$. Thus $v_p(X)\ge e$. This argument applies separately to each
entry of the mixed order list.

In particular $v_p(\varepsilon)\ge1$, where $\varepsilon=\theta^2-2$.
Hensel lifting gives a root $\rho$ of two congruent to $\theta$ modulo $p$;
thus $p$ splits and $\theta+\rho$ is a unit. If
$v_p(\varepsilon B),v_p(A+B\theta)\ge e$, then
$v_p((\theta-\rho)B)\ge e$, so $v_p(A+B\rho)\ge e$.
The order-one $f$ tests therefore put all primary points in the formal
group at this place; the conjugate tests put $J$ and all differences in
the formal group at the opposite place. Here $v_p(f)>0$ means
$v_p(x)<0$, which is the formal branch of the good Weierstrass model.

Write $Q_0=hP_*$ and $Q_i=m_iP_*$ at this prime, and let
$(n_1,n_2,n_3,n_4)=(n,s,t,z)$ be the target indices. The unchanged
common auxiliary point is $J=jP_*$ with $j\in\Z\setminus\{0\}$.
Formal logarithm homomorphism and isometry
\cite[IV.6.4 and VII.2.1--2.2]{silverman}, used with the same good-reduction
hypotheses as in Section~\ref{subsec:o8-common-J-proof}, identify
at the opposite place
the alternate parameter-ratio valuations with
\[
 v_p((h-4)/j)\ge64,\qquad
 v_p((m_i-4n_i)/j)\ge e_i.
\]
Since $j$ is an integer, these imply
\[
 h\equiv4\pmod {p^{64}},\qquad m_i\equiv4n_i\pmod {p^{e_i}},
 \qquad(e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4)=(16,64,64,64).
\]
In particular $h$ is a $p$-unit. Formal logarithm homomorphism gives
$\log_E(Q_i)/\log_E(Q_0)=m_i/h$. The relative estimates in
Lemma~\ref{lem:quartic-reciprocal-log}, followed by the primary tests,
therefore give integrality and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:quartic-mixed-congruences}
 \beta\equiv n\pmod {p^{16}},\qquad
 (\xi,\tau,\zeta)\equiv(s,t,z)\pmod {p^{64}}.
\end{equation}
The common denominator retains precision $64$ in this argument.

Put $a=|s|$, $B=\max(|n|,|s|,|t|,|z|)$ and
$\Delta=t^2-s(s-2)tz+(s-2)^2z^2-1$.
The unchanged anchor \eqref{eq:o8-anchor-bound} gives
$a>(20H)^2$. If $\Delta\ne0$, the three precision-$64$ congruences
at every contact, together with the retained proxy Lucas equation,
give the same radical divisibilities as before. They control all four
target abscissas, including that of $nP_*$. The shared-coordinate
height calculation and \eqref{eq:o8-indexheight} give
\[
 B^2-6<7H|\Delta|^{3/8}<14HB^{3/2},
 \qquad B<(14H+6)^2\le(20H)^2.
\]
This contradicts $B\ge a$. Hence $\Delta=0$, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:o8-lucas} gives $\log B>a-3$.

If $\beta\ne n$, put $N=|\operatorname{num}(\beta-n)|$ in lowest terms.
Now the precision-$16$ congruences give sixteenth-power radical
divisibilities. The unchanged height calculation yields
\[
 B^2<7HN^{3/2}+6,\qquad N\le2e^{h(\beta)}B.
\]
Since $B,H\ge1$, it follows that
\[
 B^{1/2}<(7\cdot2^{3/2}+6)He^{3h(\beta)/2}
          <32He^{3h(\beta)/2}.
\]
The scalar orders have not changed, so \eqref{eq:o8-scalarheight} gives
$h(\beta)\le H\sqrt a<a/20$. Also $\log(32H)<a/20$:
for $H\ge1$, the inequality $20\log(40H)<(20H)^2$ follows by
checking $H=1$ and differentiating the difference. Consequently
\[
 \log B<2\log(32H)+3h(\beta)<a/4<a-3,
\]
another contradiction. Thus $\beta=n\in\Z$, and reducing the
denominator in $X^2=\beta-2$ proves $X\in\Z$.

Conversely, for integral $X$ retain the choices in the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:o8-conditional}: choose the scalar height data, an anchored
$S$ with the required divisibilities, the Lucas indices, a denominator
for the eight abscissa coefficients, and the ordinary prime pattern.
Fix the same orientations as in Section~\ref{subsec:o8-common-J-proof}.
For the finite set $\mathcal P$ of distinct selected ordinary primes, put
\[
 j=\operatorname{lcm}_{p\in\mathcal P}d_{p,2},\qquad J=[j]P_*.
\]
At each selected prime choose the private common index $h_p$ satisfying
\[
 h_p\equiv0\pmod {d_{p,1}},\qquad h_p\equiv4\pmod {d_{p,2}},
 \qquad h_p\equiv4\pmod {p^{64+v_p(j)}}.
\]
The original gcd and $p$-unit conditions prove compatibility; avoid
$0,4,-4$ as there to preserve the nonzero points and subtraction guards.
Set $Q_0=[h_p]P_*$ and $Q_i=[h_pn_i]P_*$, using the same orientation at
repeated occurrences of a prime. Their shifted differences are
$[(h_p-4)n_i]P_*$, with $n_0=1$. The primary points are formal at the
first place, and $J$ and these differences are formal at the second.
Lemma~\ref{lem:quartic-reciprocal-log} gives every required primary ratio
estimate, including the weaker beta estimate. Lemma~\ref{lem:quartic-reciprocal-nonzero}
makes the finite logarithm inverses defined. Choose the single common
$\theta$ last to meet all coefficientwise conditions, as in
Section~\ref{subsec:o8-root-proof}. The norm and pole completeness
arguments, including positivity, square reduced denominators and the
local square conditions at $2,3,17$, are unchanged. No integrality of
the private primary points at these three primes is newly required.
This constructs all witnesses. The final assertion follows from the
explicit solution maps in the next lemma.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Compressed primary charts]
\label{lem:quartic-compressed-primary}
The five primary charts at each contact can be replaced by coordinates
$u_i,v_i,f_i,x_i,p_i\in K$ satisfying
\[
 f_i=u_i^2,\qquad v_i^2+df_i=1,\qquad
 p_i^2=x_i-Df_i,\qquad x_if_i=1,
\]
with $y_i=x_ip_i$ used as an expression in the subtraction chart.
Put $G_0=G_{15}(Df_0^2)$, $G_1=G_3(Df_1^2)$, and
$G_i=G_{15}(Df_i^2)$ for $i=2,3,4$. The original four ratios have
exactly the same rational solution projection as
\[
 \Lambda p_0=G_0,\qquad A_i=C_ip_i,\qquad A_i\Lambda=G_i
 \quad(1\le i\le4).
\]
The original input coordinate and all external point coordinates are fixed.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
From a full old chart set $p_i=y_if_i$. Its equations give
$h_i=u_ip_i$ and $f_ip_i^2=1-Df_i^2$, hence the four displayed equations.
Every $p_i$ is nonzero because $x_i,y_i,f_i,z_i$ are nonzero.
Set $\Lambda=-L_{64}(Q_0)=G_0/p_0$ and $A_i=C_ip_i$.
Since $z_i=-1/p_i$, the old ratio is
$C_i=G_i/(p_i\Lambda)$, proving the new equations with the stated sign.

Conversely every $G_i$ is nonzero by
Lemma~\ref{lem:quartic-reciprocal-nonzero}. Thus $\Lambda p_0=G_0$
forces $\Lambda,p_0\ne0$, and $A_i\Lambda=G_i$, $A_i=C_ip_i$
force $p_i\ne0$ for every $i$. Also $x_if_i=1$ gives $f_i\ne0$.
The identity
\[
 f_ip_i^2=1-Df_i^2=v_i^2(1+df_i)
\]
then forces $v_i\ne0$. Reconstruct
\[
 z_i=-1/p_i,\qquad y_i=x_ip_i,\qquad
 h_i=u_ip_i,\qquad w_i=u_ip_i/v_i.
\]
These give $h_i=v_iw_i$, $w_i^2+v_i^2=2$, $z_ih_i=-u_i$,
and $y_iz_i=-x_i$, so all old chart equations hold. Put
$L_i=z_iG_i$ and restore the old common inverse as $1/L_0$.
The new equations give exactly $C_i=L_i/L_0$.

Only private primary coordinates are removed. Every occurrence of $y_i$
in a subtraction line is replaced by $x_ip_i$; its first equation is
$x_i(\lambda_i-p_i)-\eta_i=0$. All subtraction guards and all difference
parameters remain. Both common auxiliary parameters and all root point
parameters remain. Thus every external equation retains its value.
The four chart equations alone would permit $p_i=0$; it is the retained
$G_i$ equations and the proved nonvanishing that exclude this case.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Exact evaluation of the finite polynomials.}
The actual source uses the following quadratic evaluation, at scale one.
For $G_{15}$ bind five field pairs
\[
 w=Df^2,\qquad w_2=w^2,\qquad w_3=w_2w,\qquad h=w_3^2,\qquad t,
\]
where
\[
 t=h\sum_{j=12}^{15}\frac{a_j}{a_{12}}w^{j-12}
       +\frac{a_{10}}{a_{12}}w_3w+\frac{a_{11}}{a_{12}}w_3w_2.
\]
The quadratic output expression is
\[
 G_{15}(w)=a_6\left\{
 h\left(\frac{a_{12}}{a_6}t+\sum_{j=6}^{9}\frac{a_j}{a_6}w^{j-6}\right)
       +\sum_{j=0}^{5}\frac{a_j}{a_6}w^j\right\}.
\]
Here $w^4,w^5$ mean $w_3w,w_3w_2$, and $w^0,w^1,w^2,w^3$ mean
$1,w,w_2,w_3$. Substitution gives every coefficient $a_j$ in its required
degree. The constants $a_6=-418/16575$ and $a_{12}$ are nonzero.
For $G_3$, bind only $w=Df^2,w_2=w^2$ and use
$1+a_1w+a_2w_2+a_3w_2w$. Insert these quadratic expressions directly
into $\Lambda p_0=G_0$ and $A_i\Lambda=G_i$, without adding separate
output pairs. Thus no cubic equation is introduced. The full polynomial
identities, including both rational coefficients, specify the source
evaluation; they are not inferred from a local error estimate.

The resulting source has $12\,064$ rational coordinates, including input
zero, and $11\,499$ residuals of degree at most four. Its twenty-five
shared anchor coordinates and scalar orders are unchanged. The source
file \nolinkurl{source-residuals.jsonl.gz} in the quartic package has SHA-256
\begin{center}\footnotesize\ttfamily
ce9eeac7c4730aced8cfb70a1ab3b1b6a7fb2110c597afad1f56ddc92aeea73f.
\end{center}
The uncompressed source bytes have SHA-256
\begin{center}\footnotesize\ttfamily
b5e836d7764363fcbfdafbacefe80a5f53e0979eba73af990827942b0fa9351d.
\end{center}
The entry \nolinkurl{source-entry.json} gives it the distinct name
\nolinkurl{reciprocal64-beta16-compressed-s1-b5e836d77643}.
Its \nolinkurl{source/} directory contains the six modules, shared chain,
flattened constraints and compiler copies. The base builder is retained
as construction machinery, with the original comparison regenerated
against its full canonical digest before the revision is installed.
The independent source audit checks all core equations after expanding
arithmetic definitions, every ordered call argument, the frozen modules,
and the complete flattening. These finite checks are separate from
Theorem~\ref{thm:quartic-source-arithmetic}.

\subsection{Quadratic reductions preserving the rational input projection}
\label{subsec:quartic-reductions}

We describe the algebraic reductions applied to the new, fixed source.
All scalar coordinates range over $\Q$, and coordinate zero is the original
input $X$. Each field equation denotes its two rational coefficient
equations. These reductions prove equality of rational input projections
to that source; its arithmetic interpretation is
Theorem~\ref{thm:quartic-source-arithmetic}.

\paragraph{Definitions, row operations, and interfaces.}
An equation $cv-F=0$, with $c\in\Q^*$ and $F$ independent of $v$,
permits substitution $v=F/c$ in every other equation and deletion of $v$.
Restriction is the forward solution map, and adjoining $v=F/c$ is its
inverse. Each use below retains degree at most two after substitution.
The initial quadratic lift uses the reverse operation: introduce targets
for products of two available coordinates until the source residuals are
quadratic. Evaluating these product definitions and forgetting their
targets give the two solution maps. A previously defined product can be
reused only with its retained defining equation.

An operation replacing $R_i$ by $aR_i+bR_j$, while retaining $R_j$,
has inverse $R_i=(R_i'-bR_j)/a$ when $a\ne0$ and $i\ne j$.
Thus every recorded linear row operation preserves the simultaneous zero
set. A shear replaces an old witness by $v=v'+cw$, with fixed rational
$c$ and another witness $w$ retained. Its forward and reverse coordinate
maps are $v'=v-cw$ and $v=v'+cw$. This is an invertible rational coordinate
change and preserves quadratic degree.

Every removed internal coordinate must have no occurrence outside the
replaced rows, unless the stated substitution is made in \emph{every}
such row. Retained coordinates keep their identities and values. All new
coordinates are fresh, and input coordinate zero is never a target of
deletion or redefinition. These conditions apply to the current system
after all preceding transformations.

\paragraph{Norm inverses.}
For rational affine expressions $A,B$, replace the constraint
$u(A^2-2B^2)=1$ and its private lifting definitions by
\[
 As+2Bt=1,\qquad At+Bs=0.
\]
The forward assignment is $s=Au$, $t=-Bu$; the reverse assignment is
$u=s^2-2t^2$. The identity
\[
 (A^2-2B^2)(s^2-2t^2)=(As+2Bt)^2-2(At+Bs)^2
\]
proves the reverse implication. All other private lifting coordinates
are reconstructed through their old definitions. No additional
nonvanishing premise or square-root choice is used.

\paragraph{Private rational inverse guards.}
Suppose the retained equations include
\[
 \varepsilon=\theta^2-2,\qquad R(F-1)=\varepsilon^2.
\]
Rational nonsquareness of $2$ gives $\varepsilon\ne0$ and hence $R\ne0$.
If a rational coordinate $u$ occurs only in $uR=1$, remove it and that
equation. The reverse map $u=1/R$ is defined on every remaining solution.

\paragraph{Two reductions of the point chart.}
Each retained full root chart has field coordinates $u,v,w,z,f,h,x,y$ and equations
\[
 f=u^2,\quad v^2+df=1,\quad w^2+v^2=2,\quad h=vw,
 \quad zh=-u,\quad xf=1,\quad yz=-x.
\]
Replace the private coordinates $w,h$ by $p$ and use
\[
 f=u^2,\quad v^2+df=1,\quad p=yf,\quad p^2=x-Df,
 \quad xf=1,\quad yz=-x.
\]
Forward, put $p=yf$. The inverse and parameter equations give
$x,f,u,y,z\ne0$. From $zh=-u$ one obtains $xh=yu$ and $h=up$.
Therefore
\[
 fp^2=h^2=v^2w^2=(1-df)(1+df)=1-Df^2,
\]
which proves $p^2=x-Df$. Conversely, the new equations give $p\ne0$
and $fp^2=v^2(1+df)$. Thus $v\ne0$. Define
\[
                         h=up,\qquad w=up/v.
\]
Then $h=vw$, $w^2=1+df=2-v^2$, and
$zh=zu yf=-u$. These formulas reconstruct the old coordinates exactly.
Both systems are quadratic in rational components; for example the
two new equations $p^2=x-Df$ are
\[
 p_0^2+2p_1^2=x_0-11f_0+12f_1,\qquad
 2p_0p_1=x_1+6f_0-11f_1.
\]

In a second step, retain $xf=1$, replace $p=yf$ and $yz=-x$ by
$pz=-1$, and substitute $y=xp$ in every outside equation.
Indeed the old equations imply both new relations, while adjoining
$y=xp$ gives $yf=p$ and $yz=-x$. This step is used only where all
substituted equations remain quadratic. For example a subtraction line
$\lambda x-y=\eta$ becomes $x(\lambda-p)=\eta$. No outside occurrence
of either rational component of $y$ is omitted.

\paragraph{A quadratic presentation of the parity block.}
This replacement concerns only its rational equations, with unchanged

This establishes the degree, monomial count, occurrence of every variable,
and exact coefficient maximum. A small coefficient bound for a local
replacement is insufficient by itself: the full expansion includes all
repeated instances and all cross terms. These finite checks prove the
algebraic conversion and its numerical assertions, not the source height
estimate or other arithmetic theorems.

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:quartic}]
For each fixed rational value of $X_0$, the initial product definitions and
the displayed solution maps preserve the existence of rational witnesses
at every recorded transformation. The simultaneous vanishing of the final
residuals is therefore equivalent to that of the pinned source residuals.
The latter is equivalent to $X_0\in\Z$ by
Theorem~\ref{thm:o8-conditional}. Since the final polynomial is the
unweighted sum of the residual squares, it has exactly the same rational
input projection. The complete integer expansion gives the stated counts
and coefficient maximum. It contains a nonzero degree-four term, so the
degree is exactly four.
\end{proof}

The quartic has the same arithmetic dependencies as its source. The
conversion does not replace the preceding proofs of those dependencies.
